text: This lab is a worked scenario from start to finish, built entirely from what the last three lessons already gave you — no screenshots, just the real sequence of decisions, applied carefully to one real stakeholder request.

The Service Desk Manager sends a request: one place to check every morning, showing how bad the current backlog is and which team is carrying it. That's two separate questions, which means two separate reports, assembled onto one dashboard, and visible only to the Service Desk Manager role.

Both questions run against the same table and the same filter — the incident table, filtered to active records only. How bad is the backlog becomes a Pie chart grouped by Priority. Which team is carrying it becomes a Bar chart grouped by Assignment group instead. Same table, same filter, different group-by field, different chart type — that's the entire difference between the two reports.

Each report gets built and saved independently in Report Designer first, with clear names like Open Incidents by Priority and Open Incidents by Assignment Group. Only after both exist do you open the Dashboard application, create a new dashboard, and add both as widgets on the same tab, resizing them so both are visible at once.

The last step is the one it's easiest to skip. Set a refresh interval if this dashboard is meant to stay open on a screen all day, and restrict its visibility to the Service Desk Manager role — a backlog-and-staffing view, not something every end user needs to see. Setting that restriction now, deliberately, is what keeps the dashboard reaching exactly the audience it was built for.

Table, filter, group-by, chart type, assembly, visibility — every decision in this lab traces back to a lesson you already have, which is exactly the point: a real request is rarely a brand-new concept, it's a familiar sequence applied carefully.
